Chapter 3 96
Enriching with tags from your infrastructure
Most infrastructure teams have worked out a good way to tag their infrastructure. When
creating new virtual machines through IaC tools such as Terraform, Ansible, Chef, or AWS
CloudFormation, the individual server instance typically follows a naming scheme but is
enriched with tags that indicate why this infrastructure exists, what its purpose is, and who
owns it. Here's an example:
Name: foneacme_p_w_csp_web3
Environment: Production, Dev, Staging
Group: Web, DevTools, BusinessApps, Backoffice
Application: CustomerServicePortal, OnlineBanking, TimeManagement, Salary,
SalesPortal
Project: Project-A, Project-B, Project-C
Owner: CustomerService, Engineering-TeamA, LOB-OnlineBanking, SalesUSEast, CFO
CostCenter: Dev, Sales, Finance, LOB
To learn more about good tagging strategies, please consult the available white papers and
best practices documentation of your cloud partner, such as the Best Practice for Tagging AWS
Resources[1].
When ingesting logs, metrics, traces, or any type of events (deployment, configuration,
security, and so on), the best practice is to enrich those signals with the same tags. This
ensures proper filtering, alerting, and access control, which is all managed through all the
already-available tags and doesn't need to be configured on top of the metadata that already
exists. To continue the previous example, let's discuss two scenarios.
Use case: logs only accessible for sales
If logs from the sales portal backend are ingested with the Owner:SalesUSEast tag, then these
logs are most likely only for the eyes of the sales organization of that region, as well as for the
global sales team. The backend observability storage can be set up so that all logs with that tag
can only be seen by those team members by specifying what some observability vendors refer
to as the security context.

Use case: traces from development only kept for two sprints
When ingesting traces in the lower-level development environments, and those traces are
enriched with the Environment:Dev tag, they may only be stored for two sprints. Why?
Because traces captured during a development cycle are typically only relevant for the time
when active development is done. Most developers don't need traces from their development
environment at a later time. So, retention of those traces can be set to a shorter timeframe, and
with this, the organization can save on observability storage and retention costs.
Think about your own current tagging strategy for your infrastructure and make sure that
those tags can be used to enrich any ingested observability signal, including logs, metrics,
traces, events, real idx_10abe610 user data, and profiling.

When analyzing metrics, logs, or traces, we can now compare the difference in response time,
execution behavior, memory consumption, or error logs between different versions of a service.
If the team decides to push a new version to a group of customers, they can now selectively
analyze and compare those signals. Additionally, we can leverage AI and automatic anomaly

This allows the team to quickly roll back to the more stable version.

good enough for production?
Ingesting deployment signals enriched with metadata from all environments (development,
quality assurance, preproduction, and production) also makes it easy to compare versions. Too
often, the question comes up: " Will the new version we have in preproduction be better than what
we have in production? " By having the metadata on logs, metrics, and traces, you can actively
compare idx_b1fa3ee6 performance, errors, and runtime behavior to make a more informed decision about
promoting a new version from preproduction to production.

know that a log, metric, or trace comes from a specific data center region, cluster, namespace,
workload, pod, or service. We can even enrich it with information about our release version or
deployment stage.

dive deeper and explain what problems it solves.

Use case: automated correlation of deployment changes with problems
When ingesting deployment or configuration change events into the same observability
backend that monitors the health of the deployed components, we can automatically correlate
those changes to detected problems. This allows us to automatically answer the question: " Did
my Git commit break production? "
Besides automatically correlating the event to a problem and identifying it as the potential root
cause, we can also set up automation that can immediately open up a new pull request that
suggests rolling back the change that is currently causing an issue. Mature organizations often
adopt this as a standard approach to automated remediation.
A side benefit of integrating our DevOps tools into observability by having them send events on
critical life cycle idx_01482f12 stages is that we can expand on this and also idx_7c58e748 observe these tools in terms of
health and activity. After all, nothing is worse for a development team than having the
supporting tools fail when they are most needed.
Observing your DevOps tools
" Why is Jira so slow today? Why is my latest code change still not running through our build pipeline?
Why do I keep getting errors when using our Visual Studio Code AI agent for code reviews? "
Sometimes the idx_5cdb5aa0 answers to these questions are idx_cbe7735c straightforward. It could be that Jenkins
pipelines are taking longer to execute because of a shared infrastructure issue. Jira might be
unavailable because of a misconfigured network route, or a misconfigured MCP server might
have executed too many GitHub API calls, causing your other users to run into rate limiting.
While those answers sound simple, they are typically not identified automatically, but only
when people have been impacted and started to complain.
Thanks to the broader adoption of open standards such as OpenTelemetry, we see better
observability support built into all those tools. This allows us to apply the same observability
practices on those tools as we apply to our business-critical apps.
Ideally, you should also set up observability with proper alerting for your Jira, GitHub, GitLab,
Argo, Harbor, and similar tools. This gives you the chance to fix problems before they impact
the majority of your engineers.

Chapter 3 102
Quality of data: where to enrich it and what to sample
We have talked a lot idx_0b81192c about how we need to enrich observability data by providing more
context across the stack and the SDLC. The remaining questions are about where to enrich our
logs, metrics, traces, and events, and how to strike the right balance between capturing
everything and capturing what we need, to control costs and make data analysis more
efficient.
How and where to enrich observability data with context
Enriching observability data close to the source, where it gets generated, is the best and most
efficient way to increase the quality of your observability data. Quality is what matters once we
start discussing how the observability data can be analyzed using machine learning or AI. As
the saying goes: garbage in, garbage out.
The same is true for observability data. Only if the observability data is of good quality and
enriched with additional context will we be able to leverage the full potential of AI. Why?
Because, like humans, AI will produce better outcomes on better observability data.
In other words: high-quality observability in, high-quality insights out.
Depending on the tooling used for collecting observability data, there are different options for
when and where to enrich it. Observability agents from vendors typically enrich the logs,
metrics, traces, and events right where the agent picks up those signals. For example,
Dynatrace's OneAgent has the option to enrich the data right at the cluster, host, or process
level. Dynatrace also has a public semantic dictionary that defines what metadata it looks for
and what it will do with the observability data once it gets analyzed[2]. A common alternative
is to use a data pipeline such as the OpenTelemetry Collector. The Collector provides so-called
processors that allow idx_9c975b86 defining rules of what additional metadata should be used to enrich logs,
metrics, or traces before they are sent to the observability backend. For best practices on
OpenTelemetry enrichment, check out the many available tutorials and best practices, such as
the GitHub tutorials from isItObservable [3].
Do we need all the data? Sampling strategies
While context-enriched idx_fa2d1ce5 data is higher in quality and easier to analyze, we also need to bring up
an important question: " Do we really need all observability data all the time? "
Think about a bank that wants to observe every single banking transaction from end to end
with logs, metrics, and traces. With potentially thousands of transactions per second, we are
talking about a lot of data. That's a lot of data that needs to be captured, enriched with context,
transmitted to the backend, stored, and later analyzed if a transaction fails. But what if only
0.1% of transactions ever fail? Do we still need the successful 99.9% in all of that detail? Or is it

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 102
chunks.content:
103 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
enough to capture a representative sample of that data in detail and just create metrics for the
total number of transactions and the response time for reporting and alerting?
These are very critical questions that we need to answer that will have a major impact on the
size and cost of the observability backend where all this data gets stored.
If we decide that we do not need all the data in all its detail, we can idx_69dc8a9b apply sampling strategies.
As the name implies, sampling is about making a decision on which observability data should
be part of the sample that we look at and store, and which is ignored because it doesn't give us
any additional value.
The topic of observability data sampling is too big to cover as part of this book. There is plenty
of literature and best practices available from the OpenTelemetry community. Observability
vendors also provide good documentation about the sampling strategies that their agents or
data pipelines provide. Some of them provide basic percentage-based sampling, while others
provide highly sophisticated sampling by dynamically adjusting sampling rates based on
observed behavior in logs and traces of individual service endpoints, workloads, or
infrastructure components.
If you go down the route of implementing your data pipeline yourself and decide not to use
agents with built-in automated sampling strategies, be aware that you have to take care of
sampling yourself! For that, you need to become familiar with the available strategies in the
tools you are using.
As a reference, please review the following key sampling strategies and their approaches:
Probabilistic sampling: You idx_68dc1e9d define a certain percentage (e.g., 5%) of traces you want to
sample, meaning that you want to store them. It's efficient, and with a large volume of
data, there is a good chance that that 5% includes important traces such as those that
commonly fail or take long. If you have a small number of failed or slow requests,
chances are high that you don't capture the details for those outliers!
Adaptive sampling: The sampling rate automatically adjusts based on incoming
traffic. This avoids collecting too much additional information during peak loads and,
with that, causing any type of issues, either where the data gets captured, on the
network where the data gets transported, or in the observability backend where the
data needs to be stored and analyzed.
Rule-based sampling: You can configure what is important and what is not based on
attributes such as specific URLs, requests that tend to take longer than a certain time or
fail, or requests from specific IP address ranges. The challenge here is configuring and
maintaining the rules that also need to be evaluated on every single trace.

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 104
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 104
The next question is which idx_4b7fcc11 component decides on whether a certain data point gets sampled
or not. Head-based sampling decides at the root span (beginning), while tail-based sampling
decides when all spans of a trace are received. Tail-based sampling can make better decisions
because it sees the full trace and can analyze whether this trace is interesting, for example,
showing a problem or error or taking very long. The drawback, however, is that tail-based
sampling requires a lot of memory as first, all the spans need to be captured and analyzed
before a decision is made to sample or not. This can become very resource-intensive in large-
scale, highly distributed, and high-volume environments. Head-based sampling, on the other
hand, makes the decision at the start of a trace. This is low effort but is limited to making
decisions only based on information that is known at the beginning of a trace.
A good rule of thumb is to start with head-based sampling and then maybe combine it with
tail-based sampling for critical transactions where you need all the details for failed
transactions or where you need specific details for regulatory or compliance reasons.
To learn more, we highly recommend another tutorial from isItObservable: Sampling Best
Practices in OpenTelemetry [4].
The systems we need to manage will continue to get bigger. We need to apply the same
practice of treating our monitored entities as cattle and no longer pets, just like we did with
classical infrastructure. We need to leverage the existing metadata and enrich our observability
signals to provide a unified experience based on a well-understood semantic dictionary. Also,
we must go beyond just observing our applications; we must also observe the tools that make
changes to our software—ideally, from the first requirements definition, when the first code
gets written, tested, and deployed, until the software gets retired. This highly enriched data
will allow us to better leverage observability data for AI and machine learning. It will give us
better idx_32c1c0d5 and faster insights into ever more complex distributed systems, especially when they
don't operate as expected.
So, let's see how this can look in action.

cause detection

in our payment service. We also see new logs containing java.lang.abcdException in the frontend

Step 1: detecting abnormal events
Our journey starts with idx_ce6aba74 detecting abnormal behavior across all relevant indicators. In the
Beyond CPU and memory: cloud-native golden signals section, we discussed that we need to look
at metrics across all layers (from top to bottom):
Application: The four golden signals of external APIs, concurrent users, and user
behavior
Business service: The four golden signals of internal APIs, resource consumption, and
costs
Platform service: Wait times, queue lengths, throughput, and rate limits
Workload: Request limit usage, percentage of Pods failing, and connection timeouts
Orchestration: Kubernetes API health, number of pending Pods, and scheduling
latency
Resource: Network Ingress/Egress and compute, storage, and memory utilization
Whenever we detect an anomaly on any of those indicators because a static threshold or
dynamic baseline was breached, we can consider this as an abnormal event for a specific
component in a specific layer of our stack.
Let's visualize this with a simple example. Let's say that we have a customer-facing web app
that needs an external-facing business API for user login. This business API is slower than
usual and impacts the application's end user performance. That API is implemented by one of
our business services running on a specific Kubernetes cluster. The API depends on a queuing
platform service and communicates with a database as well. All of these services share
resources such as network, memory, and CPU as they are all deployed on the same shared
hardware. The following figure shows how we could visualize this in a heatmap dashboard. We
have all our idx_84fb8829 key indicators across our stack on the y axis. On the x axis, we visualize the state of
each indicator in one-minute intervals. The state is represented with good=green,
degraded=yellow, and fail=red. This visualization allows us to observe a handful of patterns

Here are some observations when looking at the heatmap:
There is a problem at time interval 4 that impacts pending Pods, but it has no impact on
the business or application layer.
The business API performance always degrades one minute after the database query

The business API performance recovers when the database impact is short. However, in

Visualizing abnormal behavior is most effective when done on key indicators over time.
Putting this information on a dashboard based on our architecture makes it possible for the
human eye to detect patterns rather easily. In the preceding example, it looks like the problem
is related to a database query time issue, which impacts the business API and subsequently the
application's performance for the end user. However, there are a few limitations to this
approach, which we will review next.
Scope
This is an extremely idx_2c22bb1f minimalistic example, as we are only looking at a small number of
indicators for a very specific API endpoint. In a real-world scenario, we may have hundreds of
applications and thousands of API endpoints, each using many shared platform services.
Modern observability, therefore, needs to be able to analyze potentially millions of different
data points. The challenge is not generating a lot of noise by alerting on false positives, false
assumptions, or anomalies that do not have a business impact.
•
•
•
•
109 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Dependencies
Talking about wrong assumptions, consider the preceding example where we assumed that
the business API is impacted by the database query time. In a distributed system, however,
there are many more dependencies between components that also need to be analyzed. It
could have been a coincidence that the database query time slowed down at the same time as
the business API. We haven't looked at other factors. It could be that the business API queried a
lot of data from the database service, hence the service was slower in its response. Fetching
more data also means more data kept in memory, which means more pressure on GC, which
can result in performance degradation. As you can see, there are too many data points that
need to be investigated that we can't easily fit into a table such as the one in Figure 3.13.
Shared resources
The business API shares resources with other services on the same cluster. We haven't looked
at any noisy neighbors that may impact the performance of our business API. Network traffic is

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 108
chunks.content:
shared between all components running on shared infrastructure. We haven't investigated
how network latency has impacted our service, the database service, or any other dependent
component. Dependencies and shared services can both be extracted from the context-
enriched metadata we discussed earlier. Additionally, we can use information from distributed
tracing to see the transactional dependencies from one service to other services. All of this data
needs to be considered to improve the accuracy of alerting. It also allows reducing the noise as
we can aggregate anomalies that we know result from dependent systems.
External events
So far, we have only looked at indicators from within the layers of our stack. In the Enriching
observability data across the SDLC section, we discussed the importance of ingesting events from
our delivery or configuration change tools. We could have missed a configuration change of the
request and resource limits for the business API to give another API more CPU and memory.
Such a change could result in CPU throttling of the business API and, therefore, result in
performance degradation.
The point of all of this is that we need to detect anomalies across the stack. Yet, anomalies
alone that are not enriched with information about dependencies, shared resources, and
external events will idx_9951a693 only allow us to carry out guesswork. We need all this context-enriched
data, as discussed in the previous section, to have all of the evidence available. Only then can
we scale our observability and feed it to machine learning or various AI systems to connect all
those dots and find the real root cause of abnormal behavior.
Step 2: connecting the dots to find the root cause
In this step, we idx_3dffe1a8 explain how to walk through the observability dependency model.

chunks.content:
Chapter 3 110
In Chapter 1, in the Observability and distributed systems section, we discussed how knowing the
dependencies across the vertical and horizontal stacks will allow us to quickly point to the
technical root cause of a problem that impacts our end users, our API consumers, or our SLAs.
Borrowing that same visualization from Chapter 1 but applying it to our use case from the
previous section makes it easier for us to see dependencies, cross-impacts from shared
resources, and external events.
Figure 3.14 – Finding the root cause requires connecting all abnormal events across the full stack, considering
dependencies and shared services
The preceding figure highlights how modern observability becomes more effective with
context-enriched observability data. Thanks to metadata on logs, metrics, traces, and events,
we can better analyze the cause and effect across the vertical and horizontal stacks. Since we
are able to ingest and analyze lots of data at scale, we are no longer limited to just one
application. Instead, we can, and have, to go across all applications and services to detect any
type of cross-dependencies. Let's break this down.
Horizontal stack, or call chain
Which service calls which other services, and how does the response of the callee (latency,
failure rate, and throughput) impact the caller? For example, we can learn how database query
time or the number of database rows returned impacts the performance of the business API
call.
Vertical stack, or runs on another component
Which component runs on or within another component, and how does this impact the
component itself? For example, we can learn how the GC of the Java runtime impacts the
performance idx_f078d9b5 behavior of the business API, and how the GC itself is impacted by the resource
and request limits enforced by the orchestration layer.
111 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Network connectivity
How is the distribution of components across local, remote, and cloud networks impacted? We
can learn how the quality of a network impacts point-to-point connections made between
business and platform services.
Cross-application or cross-stack
Figure 3.14 also brings in a new player: another application or another stack that relates to the
part of the system that the line-of-business application cares about. If we only focus on the
information we know about but not about the systems around it, we might never find the real
root cause. We may point to the database, but the database itself might be impacted by other
services that put it under too much stress.
With the new contextual information around vertical, horizontal, network, and cross-stack
dependency, we would probably point to the problem as being the database, but we can also
say, with high confidence, that the root cause is the reporting service that gets triggered on a

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 110
chunks.content:
schedule by an internal batch job. This job is also causing the database to slow down for our
business API, which in turn causes problems for the end user.
For our final and idx_721577aa last point, we can collect all this information with observability, but how can
we make this more explainable?
Step 3: explaining all the evidence
Not everyone can idx_8e4538f3 constantly draw diagrams about how components are related and how the
evidence trail of abnormal events leads to identifying the root cause of a known problem.
This is where automation can help us. Everything that was explained in the Step 2: connecting
the dots to find the root cause section can be automated. Many observability platforms already do
this today by connecting all the observability data, thanks to the metadata, and then following
the dependency trees as we did. Some do it more efficiently than others, as the speed heavily
depends on data quality, as well as how efficiently observability data is stored, can be accessed,
can be connected, and can be analyzed.
In whatever way you decide to implement your anomaly and root cause detection, a key step
toward making this data more actionable and ensuring our users see the value is being able to
take all this data and make it explainable in a way that humans can easily understand without
having to be an expert. What can this look like?
Look at Figure 3.15. It shows the evidence trail of a JavaScript error rate increase problem,
including information about the dependencies, a list of detected anomalies, and external
events that have a high possibility of being relevant to the root cause analysis. When putting
an LLM on top of this data, we get a good explanation of the problem, its root cause, and
recommended actions:

Now that we have seen how modern observability can be put to use by leveraging a
combination of idx_217e896c baselining, machine learning, and AI, it's time to address one challenge that AI
can't solve without our help: providing business context to better assess which anomalies are
more important than others because they impact your SLOs if you don't react fast enough.
From ops to business: SLO-based impact analysis
Imagine we are idx_3efde8d1 reliability engineers in an organization, and the following statement is our
team's operational reality:
" Since we have rolled out the new observability platform across all our applications and stacks, we
receive hundreds of incidents per day. Our teams are overwhelmed and question the value of the new
platform. It seems we are getting notifications for everything, but we don't know what is really business
relevant. Please fix this situation."
Anomaly detection, as explained in the previous section, does what the name implies: it
detects abnormal behavior. This could be an increase in queue wait time in Apache Kafka, an
increase in HTTP 500 response codes on an API endpoint, or a drop in incoming requests from
a certain IP address range. In large enterprises with hundreds or thousands of applications, it's
common for there to be hundreds or even thousands of anomalies detected per week, even
when applying all the best practices that we have outlined until this point in the book.
The question is: which of those problems do we focus on?
The right questions to ask!
Are customers impacted? Are we losing money? Are we violating our SLAs and potentially
getting fined? These idx_0051850c are the questions that IT operations and SRE teams need to ask to know
which problems they need to jump on right away and which other problems can be put aside
for now.
Instead of answering those impact analysis questions when each problem is detected, we can
use the concept of SLOs to define what our own expectations, or the expectations of our end
users, are toward our system. Once we have those SLOs, for example, 99.999% availability of a
core business API endpoint, we can prioritize those anomalies based on whether they impact
an SLO.
Moving from technical to business objectives
As we discussed, modern idx_1c2188a8 cloud-native observability must expand beyond looking at the CPU
and memory for infrastructure alerting; we must also expand our thinking of SLOs from its
original definition to looking at the four golden signals: availability, throughput, latency, and
resource consumption. Modern observability must look at business signals such as the number

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 112
chunks.content: of active users, number of orders placed, time to process claims, or revenue at risk.

chunks.heading: Chapter 3 114
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 114
In this final section, we will go a bit deeper into the reasons why you may drown in incidents at
the beginning. You will then learn the basic concepts of SLOs, how to expand from technical to
business objectives, and how they can be used in incident response to focus on anomalies that
have a potential business impact.
Why we still drown in incidents
If you need to defend why idx_480623c9 your observability implementation produces more incidents than
you'd hope, the following sections will give you enough explanation for why that is, as we have
seen this in many projects that we have worked with.
Expanded scope
Many organizations that move to a new observability platform often use this as an opportunity
to expand to more layers of their stack and expand to more applications. That's why more data
is suddenly available. More data also means more anomalies detected and, therefore, results in
more initial incident noise.
Tool consolidation
Moving to a new observability platform typically means replacing one or several existing point
solutions that were used for specific applications or specific layers of the stack. Those tools
often didn't automatically alert but were just used for troubleshooting in case of a wider issue.
All of this additional data now feeds into the anomaly detection and can increase the initial
incident noise.
Gaps in end-to-end observability
In the previous section, we showed the importance of having end-to-end observability.
Remember the database that was overloaded by a backend batch job and impacted a business
application? If we didn't have the insight that the database is used by those two applications,
we would have ended up with three incidents instead of one, as our anomaly detection would
see a problem in the business app, the batch job, and the database itself. But it would be able to
connect it all together and treat it as a single anomaly.
When organizations start to roll out modern observability, the same problem often happens.
They have some blind spots or observability gaps until the system is fully rolled out. This gap is
what can result in initial incident noise.
115 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Missing ownership
Ideally, incidents are automatically assigned to the right team that has to take action to fix the
problem. But who is responsible for a component? In the Context is king: the quality of
observability data section, we discussed the importance of enriching our data with ownership
so that we know which teams own an application, services, or a cluster. In many organizations,
this information is initially not available, or at least not easily available for the observability
platform. In that case, all new detected incidents get assigned to a fallback team, which is

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 114
chunks.content:
typically the IT operations or SRE team. You can imagine that those teams feel overwhelmed
when all of a sudden they get a lot more incidents than before. Defining ownership is therefore
key to reducing incident noise.
Lack of criticality and business impact
Not every anomaly is equal, but most often, every detected anomaly is treated the same if we
don't have the information on whether the impacted system has high or low criticality and
whether there is a potential business impact. Having this information allows automatic
filtering and routing of detected problems. Those with low criticality, for example, a slowdown
on an internal reporting service, can be assigned a lower-priority incident response process.
Those that impact our business, for example, when our users can no longer log in, should be
elevated as they need immediate attention, as this could have a very negative impact on our
reputation and revenue.
Context is again king. One best practice is to assign a criticality tag to each component, for
example, high, medium, or low. Once we detect a new anomaly, we can analyze the criticality
of the components impacted, and with that, steer the incident response process; for example,
use the highest criticality as the default value for the incident ticket that gets created.
But what about business impact? Is there a way to better quantify this than just low, medium,
and high? Is there idx_27b027b2 a way to factor in the risk or potential lost revenue for every minute our
systems are suffering from a problem?
The answer is yes! This is where SLOs and SLAs come in. SLOs allow us to specify the expected
system behavior over time, and we can use this to measure how far off we are from expected
behavior, for example, 99% uptime over 30 days, or 95% of critical API response time must be
faster than 500 ms. What are SLAs then? Well, they are like SLOs but are typically written
down in contracts as they define what happens if we do not meet our objectives. A good
example would be having to pay a penalty if we fail to deliver the uptime we promised. If you
think about banks, they need to guarantee a certain level of availability. If they don't meet it,
they need to pay penalties or they will potentially lose their banking license.

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 116
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 116
There is a lot of literature around SLAs and SLOs. We highly recommend reading the Google
SRE handbook, which does a great job of explaining the core principles behind SLIs, SLOs,
SLAs, error budgets, and burndown rates[5].
In the following sections, we will only cover SLO basics, but we will explain how SLOs allow us
to elevate our impact idx_ce8ccd1c analysis from purely technical (is it available? Is it fast?) to answer
questions such as is it highly critical because we are negatively impacting our business objectives?
A primer on SLOs: learnings from Google's SRE handbook
We don't need yet another idx_de302147 book about idx_ca082d02 SLOs as there is plenty of material available. There are
also many different tool vendors and even open standard initiatives around how to define and
calculate SLOs. We therefore suggest you read up on this information.
The most important guideline we want you to take away is: You do not need an SLO for
everything! Sounds harsh, but we have seen organizations that have tried to define 10,000+
different SLOs across their applications. They followed some of the information they read too
literally and defined the four golden signals with custom thresholds and alerts on every service
endpoint in their organization.
Let's quickly recap the basics of SLOs so we understand what we are talking about when we
use terms such as SLI, SLO, SLA, error idx_a1a56f46 budget, and burndown rate.
We will use the example of defining the SLO for the request success rate of a particular API
endpoint.
Service-level indicator
The SLI is the metric idx_e5d33d25 for understanding the health of our objective. The SLI is typically a rate
metric that delivers a value between 0 (fail) and 100 (pass). In most scenarios, we calculate
this ratio by dividing the "good events" (for example, successful API calls) across all valid
requests (for example, all measured API calls). The following is a full example of defining an SLI
for the request success rate, where we divide the total number of HTTP requests that return a
status code of 200 by the total number of requests:
Figure 3.16 – The SLI is a metric to understand the health of a component
117 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
We ideally normalize the SLI to a value between 0 and 100 as this will make it easier to define
our objective, the SLO.
Service-level objective
Building on top of idx_9c40ccea the SLI, we can idx_787b1529 define what the objective of that metric is over a specific
time period. In our example, we could specify that the request success rate should be 99.98%
over a certain observed time period. This means we want to ensure that 99.98% of requests are
returning an HTTP 200 status code and that we only allow 0.02% of requests to return a value

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 116
chunks.content:
other than HTTP 200.
Figure 3.17– The SLO defines our objective for a metric over a period of time
The SLO is really defining the threshold—or the expected value—for the SLI. Besides a single
threshold, we often also see a idx_f10b3c5b warning and an error threshold to differentiate more granularly,
not just success or failure.
Error budget and burndown rate
Once we have our idx_1f23deac SLI and idx_f860a661 the threshold for the SLO, we can calculate how much room we have
for error without violating our defined objective. This is what we call an error budget. It's also
often referred to as 100 – SLO. In other words, it's the percentage of time that we allow the
system to not work before we violate our SLO. The following figure depicts a simple calculation
of what that means if our SLO has a threshold of 99.9%. It means that for 0.1% of the time, we
are allowed to not be available or not be as fast as we should be (depending on what the SLI
measures).
Figure 3.18 – Error budget is the time we allow the system to not meet our objective

chunks.content:
Chapter 3 118
Looking at those numbers often shows us how stringent a 99.9% availability target is. It really
only allows us 43.2 minutes of not meeting our SLO over the period of a year. You can easily do
the math on how that time shortens if you add more nines, for example, 99.999%.
What do we use the error budget for? Well, we can use it to make decisions on whether we can
take some risk, such idx_92c6fb73 as deploying a change that will have a short-term impact on our SLO. By
looking at the remaining error budget, we can weigh the desire to make a change against the
potential risk of violating our SLO.
While the error budget is a great indicator and reporting tool, it's the error budget burndown
rate that's more useful. It's a good tool for getting alerts in case we are burning through our
remaining error budget too fast.
Figure 3.19 – Error budget burndown rate tells us whether we are on the trajectory to violate our SLO at the end of
the reporting period
The idea behind the burndown rate is that you can trigger alerts not only when you fail to meet
your objective by the end of the reporting period but also when you are consuming your error
budget too quickly. For example, if the burn rate is too steep, it allows you to react fast to a
critical problem that eats up your error budget.
Figure 3.20 – Burndown and burn rate as good indicators of when to react to a problem
119 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
If you have idx_953271bf investigated idx_216421fb this idx_dfea6c36 area in the past, you may think: this sounds very similar to an SLA.
You are right. So, what is the difference?
Service-level agreement
Technically, an SLA is idx_c35efdfc similar to an SLO because both are used to measure the health of our
system over a period of time. A classic example is maintaining 99.999% availability of your
system to the end consumer. We can measure it in the same way as an SLI if we analyze the
ratio between when a system is available and is not available.
So, what's the difference? SLAs are typically used in contracts. When you sign up for any SaaS
service, they typically put in an SLA for availability and maybe even for performance. We also
see SLAs defined for how fast the response to problems or incidents is; for example, as a
premium customer of our SaaS service, we guarantee that in 95% of the cases, we will respond
within one hour to critical issues.
SLOs, on the other hand, are typically used internally for additional indicators. These are
typically leading indicators that, when violated, will most likely also result in an SLA violation
if we are not acting fast enough. Think about our availability SLA example. We can define
several SLOs on critical APIs that are used when users access our services. These APIs need to

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 118
chunks.content:
be available in order idx_9b774481 for the system to idx_561f60b4 be perceived as available. This is why we would typically
specify more technical and more stringent SLOs to act as an early warning signal.
From SLOs to business objectives
Availability, response idx_73c166ee time, and error rate are very common SLOs for technical services such as
login, purchase, and recommendation services. Wait time, message process time, and message
delivery success rate are typical SLOs for queuing systems that we typically find in distributed
architectures. While all those SLOs are great for technical service owners, they do not allow us
to answer a key question: is our slow service or backed-up queue impacting our end users and,
therefore, our business?
Asking business impact questions
To elevate the discussion around indicators that matter for your business, we need to take a
top-down rather than a bottom-up approach to defining SLOs. Consider a use case of a new
mobile app for a financial services company. The most important metric for the business is not
how many messages can be processed by the backend queue, but the following:
How many users are using the new app?
How many users are logging in?
How many users can make money transfers or purchase other financial products
through the app?

chunks.content:

As we get to the more technical side, the questions would be the following:
What's the rating on the mobile app store?
What's the crash rate of the app that prevents users from doing business with the
company?
These are all the right questions to define. Use observability to capture the indicators and then
apply the concept of SLOs to report and alert when we are not meeting our business objectives.
Connecting business objectives with technical objectives
The following figure is taken from the talk Tips for running successful SLO workshops in under one
hour from SLOconf 2022[6]. In the talk, a top-to-bottom approach to defining SLOs is
explained, starting with the topmost business objective and then breaking it down into leading
indicator objectives:
Figure 3.21 – Good SLOs start with business objectives that are linked to leading indicators toward the technical
implementation
From that talk from idx_dfc95e1d SLOconf, there are a couple of clear takeaways and best practices regarding
setting SLOs:
Clearly defined: Have a clear definition of the objective and why it matters.
Measurable: How do you measure that objective—through metrics, logs, and so on?
Realistic objective: What is a realistic threshold that everyone agrees is achievable?
Ownership: Who owns the objective? Who acts on it when it's violated?
Aligned with business: How do all bottom technical SLOs map to top business
objectives?
For more information about this topic, also read the blog post How to start with SLOs to align
Business, DevOps, and SREs [7].

Business impact analysis as part of incident response
Once we have idx_11e86895 our SLOs, we can expand our AIOps implementation to include business impact
analysis. For each problem detected, we can factor in which of the impacted components have
an SLO assigned to them and which don't. Assuming that components with an SLO are more
critical, we can prioritize which anomalies should get a higher priority for incident response.
Incident analysis without SLO context

following dashboard shows how to get an overview of all these problems, grouped by problem

already a good indication that there are a lot of detected anomalies that might not have an

Connecting the SLO with the incident

We have seen organizations that have reduced their incident noise by up to 90% simply by
focusing on the problems that impact their objectives.
How to start this journey
Most organizations do not yet have a good practice for defining both technical and business
objectives. You should start tracking the ratio of incidents with an SLO-based priority
assessment. This gives your organization good guidance toward defining SLOs as it will
improve the incident response process. If you continuously track how many problems are
detected and how many of them were not business-relevant because they didn't have an SLO
defined, it highlights where you have to focus on defining good SLOs.
It's a long journey, but one worth starting as it will lead to focusing on those problems that
really impact your business instead of drowning in alerts that are not relevant, which eats
away at the time you should use for innovation.
How would Financial One ACME make this transition?
As in the previous idx_513e6041 chapters, we will idx_b36d00c0 make this real by walking you through the
transformational journey of our fictitious company called Financial One ACME. How are they
coping with moving from data on dashboards and lots of static alerts toward a layered
approach of health checks applying baselining? How are they expanding to the left and
establishing an observability-driven development culture? What type of context are they
deciding to add to their observability data to enable more self-service use cases? And how do
they define business and technical objectives to make idx_c2e4d1c9 their AIOps implementation more
effective?
You will find out by reading the next chapters!

through the workings of a fictitious company that has run into problems with their current
observability practices after completing their migration to the cloud. This company is a large
organization that works in several business markets, some of which are highly regulated. The

Our fictitious company
Introducing ACME Financial idx_bd2d4f90 Services, a fictitious company that we will use to apply the
concepts in this book to real-world scenarios. ACME Financial Services is a large financial
institution that provides services across many industries, including personal investments and
savings, management of employer-provided retirement plans, business investments, and
insurance. With this diverse product portfolio, the company runs hundreds of independent
applications across the various industries that interact with each other to provide customer
services.
Being in the financial services industry means that ACME Financial Services cares deeply about
their reputation and takes anything that might diminish the company's reputation very
seriously. After all, who would want to trust a company with a poor reputation for security,
safety, or customer service with their life savings or their business?
However, reputation is not the only concern that ACME Financial Services has. Many of the
services that the company idx_a6647747 provides are in heavily regulated industries. Complying with a
regulation requires much more work than just implementing controls or processes to ensure
the regulation is met. The company also has to have thorough documentation around their
policies and procedures for that regulation to be able to prove to regulators that they are

complying and actively ensuring compliance. A failure to meet a regulation is made worse if a
regulator determines that the company's culture, policy, or procedure is inadequate to
maintain compliance with the regulation. If you're a college sports fan, you may be familiar
with this same kind of situation where a school may be found to have inadequate controls in
place to meet a regulation and gets hit with financial penalties, loss of scholarships, or even
people losing their jobs. This means that not only does a public failure of some kind risk
damage to ACME Financial Services' reputation, but it could also result in significant financial
penalties, lawsuits, or even people losing their jobs.

After the great cloud migration
ACME Financial Services has just completed their journey transitioning to the cloud. They have
ended up with a hybrid environment because of the nature of the numerous markets the
company serves, the idx_bc03927c amount of data, and internal decisions on how best to ensure compliance
with regulations. Frontend applications were re-architected to fully embrace cloud-native
design principles and transitioned completely to Kubernetes clusters running on their cloud
provider. However, not all backend systems or application data were able to migrate to the
cloud. Despite the desire to move everything to the cloud, it was decided that this would not be
practical for a number of reasons. In some cases, there weren't suitable offerings from their
cloud provider; in others, the amount of data that they would need to move was too large to
accommodate in the cloud. Finally, regulations in some markets prevented the work from
being done in the cloud.
The end result is a mixture of new and old design principles. The applications that moved to
the cloud were redesigned following cloud-native design principles. They converted single
monolithic applications into hundreds or even thousands of microservices. In addition to that,
ACME Financial Services has improved the resiliency of these applications by running them in
multiple regions and across multiple Kubernetes clusters. In addition to improved resiliency,
they have also gained improved scalability because they properly designed their microservices
to be able to scale horizontally when needed. The company has learned that, in most cases,
increasing the number of Pods, or scaling horizontally, provides results superior to their old
practice of scaling vertically, or increasing the amount of resources available for an application.
Some of the cloud-native applications have to communicate with the old monolithic
applications on-premises. However, when they planned their cloud migration, they didn't
realize what impact the cloud-native architectures and hybrid cloud environment would mean
for their observability practices, so they didn't make any changes to the observability practices
they used for monolithic applications running on-premises. The result is that despite the
improvements in idx_46c26121 resiliency and reliability, they are seeing an increase in incident resolution
times and incidents discovered by customers.

premises. As an example, services for a single product before the migration looked like this:

ACME Financial Services' current state of observability
ACME Financial Services has a very labor-intensive approach to incident management. They
have an operations team that receives and processes the events generated from all the
applications across the multiple markets that the company serves. They also monitor social
media for any indications idx_dc45c46c of problems users may be experiencing. This operations team knows
the various functions the company provides, but has only a light understanding of the
interconnected nature of the various applications. Since this team is not composed of software
developers, they look up points of contact for the various applications running across the
company when they need to get application teams involved. However, because of their limited
understanding of how the applications are connected, the operations team takes a scattershot
approach to incident management. They create a means of live communication for an incident
and contact as many application teams as they feel might have input or be impacted by an
incident, and then drive the incident to its conclusion. This results in many application team
points of contact being needlessly roped into incidents where they have no input or impact,
and the only way for an application team to be considered exempt from an incident is for them
to prove that their application is not involved with the current incident. The result is that a
large number of application teams incur work related to an incident, either because they are
directly involved and work to resolve the problem or to show that they are not involved and
can be excused. Even with this dedicated operations team, some incidents are only detected
when users complain either directly to idx_a753d095 the company or on social media.
How their observability practices became unmanageable
ACME Financial Services' observability practices were adequate while everything was on-
premises and processing was contained to idx_eddb0e12 monolithic applications. Once services moved to the
cloud, the company noticed a degradation in incident response and resolution times. They
have put together a team to study why this is occurring and the impacts, which finds the
following:
Increased alert counts: One of the first conclusions the team finds is that there is a lot
more metric data being generated when compared to before the cloud migration, and
this is resulting in significantly more alerts. When they drill down further, the team
finds that this is primarily for the following reasons:
More services are running: When the application teams split their monolithic
applications into microservices, they generally copied their alert configurations
for each microservice performing a task. This has resulted in more alerts being

100 microservices providing the same functionality.
Static alerts: The scaling strategy relied upon monitoring resources consumed
by applications and generating alerts if any watermarks (such as high CPU or
memory) were hit, and the operations team would assess whether the
application would need to scale. This same strategy has become unmanageable
now that multiple microservices have been replaced with a single monolithic

situation by implementing auto-scaling functionality using cloud provider

the alerts generated from static definitions are still elevated from what they
were before the cloud migration.
Lost traceability: When applications were running on-premises, they were monolithic
and isolated to a single task. Now that applications have been redesigned for the cloud,
a single application could consist of multiple microservices, and some of those
microservices have multiple instances running to provide redundancy or scalability. In
their microservices architecture, services have been created that are shared across
applications, creating problems in understanding which applications are at risk from
an issue with a shared service. This has caused problems with tracing the impacts from
an alert or incident because the communication graph is much more complex.
Alert fatigue: Because there are more alerts, it is harder for response teams to know
which alerts need to be responded to and which are noise. The increased number of
alerts is causing not idx_d9638f83 only alert fatigue but also members of the response teams to burn
out. The response teams are less effective and slower in dealing with incidents.
More user-detected incidents: The team also discovers that more incidents are
slipping through the cracks and being detected only when users complain. There
doesn't seem to be a single root cause for this, and the team concludes that it is likely a
result of the other issues they have uncovered. However, because users are reporting
more problems, the company's reputation is taking a hit. Senior leadership has even
asked that new metrics be created to track where incidents are detected, which does
not put the current monitoring system in a good light.
Lack of ownership: This doesn't mean that applications are running without an

There are now many more parts to an application, and it isn't clear who owns what.
An explosion of operating costs
In addition to the decline in user experience and the resulting negative impacts on ACME
Financial Services' reputation, the company's operations costs have increased significantly.
ACME Financial Services' budget idx_ef48f12c for operations used to be close to their competitors', but costs
have risen since the cloud migration, and they are now spending more on operations than their
competitors. What's even worse is that the increased operations costs are impacting other
areas of the company. The increased costs for operations are reducing funds available for new
feature development and other areas that are vital for the company to remain competitive.
ACME Financial Services' senior leadership has communicated to the entire company that the
trend of increasing operations costs needs to be reversed and that costs need to be brought
back down in line with the company's competitors.
What about regulations?
Being in the financial industry, ACME Financial Services has numerous regulations with which
they need to comply. They don't just idx_1a31bd80 have to worry about protecting their customers' privacy
and financial information; they also have to comply with regulations specific to the financial
industry, such as detecting and preventing fraudulent transactions and detecting and
reporting suspicious activity.
Complying with these kinds of regulations is not nearly as obvious and clear-cut as some other
types of regulations. The company has to be able to detect suspicious activity and either
prevent it or report it to government regulators. For example, if an account is making hundreds
of small transactions over a short period of time, this could be suspicious, especially if the
account where the transactions are occurring doesn't have a history of that kind of transaction.
Sometimes the transaction can look completely normal, except that it originated from a foreign
country that the idx_460c5ee8 government has specified should not be allowed to transact with the
country's financial services. However, just because a country might have a government in
conflict with the country that regulates ACME Financial Services, doesn't mean the company
can flatly deny transactions from that country. The transaction could be initiated from a
customer of ACME Financial Services, and thus is unlikely to be an action taken by a hostile
government. This gets complicated very quickly. If you have ever traveled to a foreign country
and had issues performing seemingly simple financial transactions, these kinds of concerns
about regulatory compliance could be part of the reason.

Of course, preventing fraudulent transactions isn't just about complying with regulations.
Nowadays, most, if not all, financial services have policies in place to protect their customers
from fraud. This not only helps bolster trust with their customers but is also a cost-saving
measure for the financial institution. If money is withdrawn fraudulently, then the financial
133 ACME Financial Services: Implementing AIOps
institution may reimburse the customer, but no one is going to reimburse the company. The
money comes out of the company's revenue.
In order to handle these kinds of situations, ACME Financial Services has developed a number
of systems to comply with regulations around suspicious activity. The problem the company
faces is that the evolution of fraud never stops. They can develop tooling to detect a specific
pattern, but once that tooling has been deployed to prevent that pattern of fraud, the criminals
will work on creating the next one. When a new fraud pattern is used by criminals, ACME
Financial Services has to do the following:
Detect the new fraud pattern: Depending on the pattern, the amount of money
involved, and whether any existing detection systems might give a hint, detecting the
fraud could be near instantaneous or possibly take a few days.
Analyze the fraudulent pattern: Detecting that something is wrong is just the first
step. Once they know something is wrong, they then have to diagnose what systems
are being exploited and how, so they can devise countermeasures.
Prevent the fraud: They have to implement something to stop it now and any future
attempts. Depending on the complexity of the method, this could be quick or take a
while to develop and test, especially if it is something that crosses multiple
applications or service industries.
While the company is diagnosing new fraudulent activity, they are losing money. Criminals are
exploiting ACME Financial Services' weaknesses to get as much money as possible before a
countermeasure is deployed. Depending on how long the process takes, both detecting the
fraudulent pattern and implementing ACME Financial Services' countermeasure, this could
easily result in losing millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars. They even face non-
financial fraud problems involving cloud provider services, where attackers try to compromise
systems and use their resources to perform things such as cryptomining.
The large amount of money lost to idx_cb7b3ff7 fraud and the dangers of regulatory non-compliance make
it clear why regulatory compliance is of supreme importance to ACME Financial Services. It's
not just about avoiding penalties from government regulators; it is also about reducing costs
for the company and maintaining trust with customers.
Controlled deployments
In addition to their efforts to migrate to the cloud, ACME Financial Services has also been

as easy idx_941e3cb9 as just changing application development team processes due to aforementioned
concerns, such as regulatory compliance and reputational risk.

The old deployment process
Before application development teams became more iterative, they would develop features and
release them together in a idx_3b8203b5 group as a new application version. They couldn't just deploy that
new version at any time of the day, though. The risks of disrupting something important
during stock market hours were far too great, so ACME Financial Services created a somewhat
laborious deployment process:
Application deployments could only be done after hours unless there was a critical bug
that needed to be fixed.
Development teams had to come up with a deployment plan, which included what was
being deployed, how long the deployment was expected to take, and how to ensure
functionality.
The deployment plan would have to be signed off on and agreed to by a leader of their
business unit.
In order for an application version to be eligible for deployment, it would first have to
pass quality checks.
Usually, new application versions were deployed about once a business quarter. While the
deployment process was somewhat onerous, it only had to be performed a few times a year.
However, with the push to develop and deploy changes more quickly using an iterative
development approach, this deployment process became a hindrance as the number of
deployments increased drastically. To make matters worse, application teams didn't discover
their deployment problems until they idx_af91eecb were late into the deployment planning process.
From continuous delivery to continuous incident
ACME Financial Services has tackled some of these problems by finding ways to automate the
deployment approvals process and shift left the discovery of deployment problems. For
example, they have implemented idx_3b9848d8 standard CI/CD practices with new builds being deployed to
non-production Kubernetes clusters and a home-grown tool that allows more deployment
automation based upon an application's test coverage and test automation. This has helped
reduce the burden of deploying a new application version, with some applications able to
achieve their highest deployment automation, which will automatically deploy to production
once non-production is ready. However, now that there are more application deployments,
there are naturally more incidents. This isn't because quality has slipped, but simply because
the complexity of the applications is growing at a faster rate, and that leads to more incidents.
With a large and complex suite of applications and some new features requiring changes
across multiple applications, the incident response teams are becoming lost in a sea of
changes.

The strain from adding features
As the number of features they roll out increases, their understanding of how well used, or
even well liked, those new features are has been decreasing. They still deploy significant
changes or new features behind configuration gates, but now there are significantly more
changes being controlled by idx_34ab1b77 these configuration gates. Because of this, it is much harder for
incident teams, or even application development teams, to know what is actually being used at
any time within the complex system of applications that make up ACME Financial Services. As
you might expect, this has led to internal strife trying to figure out whether a feature is being
used, whether it is liked, and whether it should continue to be developed or removed.
The technology stack
As part of their migration to the cloud, ACME Financial Services also consolidated and changed
their observability stack. Before the migration, the observability stack consisted of some
homegrown solutions and some idx_24e739b8 proprietary solutions. They weren't able to get rid of all of the
proprietary solutions for various reasons, but whenever possible, they moved toward open
standards. This allowed them a larger selection of tools to choose from as part of their cloud
migration journey.
One of the nice things about using a cloud provider is the large number of managed services
they tend to offer. Not only do they provide automation and management tooling around
Kubernetes clusters, but they also tend to have at least some monitoring tools. In the case of
ACME Financial Services, their cloud provider offers managed observability tooling, and this is
the path the company chose to take for their new observability technology stack.
Their cloud provider provides managed Prometheus and Grafana offerings at a reasonable
price. ACME Financial Services decided that using those tools would be more cost-effective
than running similar tooling themselves. This was a project in itself, as not only did application
development teams idx_3325f06e have to change how they created observability information, but everyone
had to be trained on how to use these new tools. By everyone, we mean not just application
development teams, but incident response teams, managers, and business leaders. It was quite
an effort.
For logs, they moved away from an on-premises solution to a cloud-based one. Even on-
premises applications send their logs to the cloud log collector. The cloud log collector

Deciding what to improve from a sea of options
ACME Financial Services has quite a few problems to address, and they are not trivial. There is

discuss, debate, and even argue over what to address first. They decide on a framework to help
guide their decisions.
The first, and most important, factor for a decision is how, and how much, the change would
reduce costs. To that end, they decide to start with the largest gaps with the current tooling
and processes. Once they identify those gaps, they need to determine how much each gap is
contributing to the increased operational expenses. With that data in hand, they will be able to
investigate solutions and compare how much those potential solutions reduce costs. Once they
have chosen their solutions, they will have to decide which improvements to tackle when. It is
unlikely they will be able, or allowed, to implement everything in the first iteration. Some
improvements may require new tools, which may require a lengthy vendor evaluation and
onboarding process. Of course, application development teams will still need to deliver new
features and bug fixes while they work toward supporting these improvements around
operational costs. Despite the mandate from senior leadership to reduce costs, it will still be
critical to align all these pieces in order for any improvement to succeed. It is no easy feat.

ACME Financial Services has taken the first, and easiest, step in improving their observability

Build versus buy
To start with, we will take a short diversion to discuss a few economic principles that can
provide insights into why sometimes idx_8a7b2d17 buying a tool can still be the better choice even if the
math says building a tool would be cheaper. We won't dive into these too deeply:
Opportunity cost: In simple terms, this is the cost of the alternative not chosen. In a
scenario where you are building a tool versus buying it, you will have to devote
resources to designing, developing, and maintaining any tool that is developed in-
house. The project will need to provide roadmaps and consume other project
management resources as any other project would. While those resources are working
on this tool, they are unable to work on functionality that might benefit the company
more directly. For example, if a tool is projected to take two years to build, along with
10 developers, a technical lead, part of a project manager, part of an architect, and so
on, then the time spent by those resources cannot be used to help create a killer
functionality to gain more customers or to fix long-standing and frustrating bugs.
Specialization: This basically means one group focuses on producing a limited set of
goods or services, which means they are able to produce it faster and cheaper. In our
example, a vendor would be well versed in the problem space they are solving and will
have cultivated the expertise needed to solve the problems. In the case of ACME
Financial Services, their expertise is in the financial sector, not in observability tooling,
let alone AI or ML.
Even with first-hand experience of those economic principles, there is still an emphasis on
building a tool instead of buying one that must be addressed. The first consideration in this
process is whether there are tools available in the open source community that can be used as a
foundation for an in-house solution, and how much functionality those tools provide toward
the overall solution.
The next area to consider is the current state of the situation at ACME Financial Services. Is the
situation dire and the solution needed as soon as possible? If so, this could make the buy
option much more attractive, but it comes with a catch. Just because a third-party tool may be
needed now, does not mean that an in-house tool couldn't be developed later. The third-party
tool may alleviate the immediate need, but the in-house tool is the desired final solution, even
once taking into account migration costs.
Lastly, they need to consider how long it will take to deploy a third-party tool. Is the tool
complicated enough that it will take significant time to plan and deploy it? ACME Financial

The traceability group
The group tackling the traceability problem idx_34050b3b wants to solve the difficulty their teams have with
understanding what is happening within an application and across applications in multiple
business areas. Currently, tracing and discovering the root cause of an incident is almost
impossible, with groups of developers needing to coordinate inspecting log entries across
multiple applications. Most of the time, the application teams have to get into a meeting and
investigate together to try to figure out how the applications interact and what is going wrong.
It is a very time-consuming and laborious process.
The team starts by looking at what tools may exist that could improve the flow of information
across the applications. They quickly come across OpenTelemetry (https://
opentelemetry.io), which is an open source project with support for many programming
languages. This seems very promising, so the team decides to focus on evaluating it.
While evaluating OpenTelemetry, also known idx_6bf94b72 as OTel, they learn about the concept of traces.
Traces are basically structured logs with additional context built in. They have something
called a span ID, which could be used to trace communication across multiple containers and
even across multiple idx_6b5208bd applications. With context propagation, the support and application
teams would be able to trace a request through all of the parts of the system and understand
exactly what happened when and where. They decide that this sounds like exactly what they
need to solve the traceability issues at hand. They learn that there's even more to OTel, though.

Best of all, OTel is open source. However, OTel doesn't provide all this functionality in a

The feature usage group
The group tackling application feature idx_1c7909e4 usage wants to help development teams understand
how the features in their apps are being used and how resources should be used during
development. For example, if a bug affects a rarely used feature, then it probably isn't a good
use of the application team's development time if there are more impactful changes that need
to be made. Without this kind of information, application teams do their best to determine
priority based on things such as the number of complaints or how long an issue has been in the
backlog.
On the surface, this doesn't seem like a problem with a difficult solution. The group determines
that they could create a policy that all new features should be enabled by an external flag, and
that enabling the feature would also enable some metrics about how and when the feature is
used. However, some concerns arise with this approach. One concern is around
standardization. Even with training, they are sure that each development team will do things
slightly differently. Another concern is how to manage the flag configurations for each
application, let alone if a feature spans multiple applications or business domains. So, they
decide to do some research to see whether there are any examples of others tackling these
problems.

discover that the project provides a way to idx_bd218dfa standardize feature flag implementations and even
supports automated support for OTel. It supports many remote flag management tools, which

languages and remote flag management server mean they will be able to manage features
across application domains. They can even coordinate feature availability to their mobile apps,
which is beyond the scope of their original ideas for a solution.

development teams, but this seems like a clear win.
The fraud group

wider set of problems, this group is idx_7f100ca6 focused on how an observability tool can help address

A user who has logged in and is trying random URL endpoints on the company's
