The SLO mess
It has long been the practice at ACME idx_88823d07 Financial Services for applications to create, monitor,
and alert on SLOs. With a growing number of applications across multiple business areas, the
number of SLOs generating alerts has exploded. Everything from a highly important interface
to a customer to applications that do processing in off-hours generates alerts when their SLO is
violated. They know that the number of applications will continue to grow, so this policy is not
going to be viable moving forward.
Knowing the policy isn't viable is one thing, but knowing what to do about it is something else.
They start researching SLO best practices and find that they need to change how they think
about SLOs. They decide to evaluate a practice of looking at SLOs from the outside in, which is
to say services and interfaces that the customer interacts with, and any systems used to
support those operations. This practice would focus on events that users would experience,
and those are the most important events to ACME Financial Services. Since they are acutely
aware of the company's reputation, this policy would help align the actions of the response
teams with the principles the company cares about the most.
Implementing this SLO practice would drastically reduce the number of SLOs being tracked
and generating alerts. It would require changing company guidelines that have stood for a long
time, but the working group is confident that they have a winning message that they can take
to senior leadership.
Static alerts
Another driver of alert fatigue is the idx_cd597862 common practice of using static alerts by the application
teams. When applications were relatively few and monolithic, this practice wasn't so bad. If an
application was low on CPU, memory, or disk availability, then the support teams would want
to know in order to take action before a failure occurred. Now that the application teams have
modernized and adopted cloud-native design principles, those same alerts are now being
generated by many more application Pods. Even worse, that same data is sometimes used to
auto-scale the Kubernetes cluster or application Pods, which means the alert is complete noise.
It seems obvious that a first step to improve the noise generated by these alerts is to remove
any alerts around metrics used to auto-scale the Kubernetes cluster or application Pods. While
that is a good start, it doesn't go nearly far enough to solve this problem. The number of Pods
generating alerts is enormous and only getting larger. These alerts also have much less utility
than they did in the past. If 1 Pod out of 100 is low on CPU, memory, or disk, that isn't as much
of a concern as when the monolithic application they replaced raises the same alert.
They decide to look into what other options exist for alerting practices besides static alerts. The

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 146
chunks.content:
working group discovers that this problem is one that ML/AI can help address. Instead of
setting static thresholds for each Pod and trying to maintain them, tools that utilize ML/AI are
147 ACME Financial Services: Implementing AIOps
able to automatically baseline an application and understand its unique usage patterns. This
can drastically cut down on the number of alerts generated. Those tools also have some other
potential benefits, such as automatically detecting relationships and anomalies, and can even
automate some response actions.
Improvement in this area would not only depend on choosing the proper tool, but also on
changing the culture and guidance for application development teams at ACME Financial
Services.
Siloed data
After talking with the response and application teams, they discover that the current processes
suffer from a problem called siloed data. The idx_32cf604a problem is that when an alert is raised, it only
provides information about a single piece idx_27cd5d17 of information. For example, the CPU utilization is
above 90%. However, once that alert has been received, there is no further indication about
what may be causing it. Prometheus has no connection to application logs or source code
repositories, so response teams and application teams have to search through logs and change
histories to try to discover what might be causing the alert. Once the alert is received, the
investigation teams have no way of knowing whether the alert was generated because of a
spike in traffic from normal usage, fraud, a long-standing bug, or a new feature that was
introduced. The lack of context for an alert means the mitigation investigation has no
definitive place to start. Some incidents benefit from tribal knowledge that teams have gained
about how an application functions and what may have caused specific problems in the past,
but that kind of information is fragile. If a person is on vacation or leaves the company, then
that knowledge isn't available when an alert is being investigated. Some teams have tried to
document this kind of knowledge in their runbooks, and while that has helped, it has not
replaced the idx_b12855e6 experience gained by those diagnosing the causes of events.
As the working group researches solutions, they discover that this is another area where
observability tooling that uses AI/ML can help. These AI/ML observability tools, combined
with OTel traces and logs, as well as source code repository commit histories, can provide a
rich set of context to response teams investigating an alert. It is exactly this kind of context
data that response teams have to go and discover on their own with the company's current
tooling.

Chapter 4 148
Alerts from logs
Even before the cloud migration effort, ACME Financial Services was already on a journey to
improve alerting within the idx_5741d744 company. The first iteration of this was going from no alerts to
using their log aggregation service to produce alerts. While this was an improvement over
nothing, it eventually came to be the bane of application and response teams. Application
teams were given free rein to decide what to alert on and at what thresholds. The application
development teams have not been diligent in trying to address the cause of alerts in non-
production environments, and so the alert notices clog up email inboxes and are largely
ignored, even in production. Most application development teams use email filters to prevent
alerts from filling up their inboxes. This is the very definition of alert fatigue.
What makes the alerts from logs even worse is that they are delayed, usually by at least 15
minutes, from the time of an event occurring. This puts response teams behind in trying to
reduce the Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR). There is a type of alert where this delay may
not matter, but for anything idx_4c3f23dd customer-facing, this guarantees that the problem will be
experienced by customers for at least 15 minutes, if not more.
For these reasons, ACME Financial Services has already been encouraging teams to move off of
log-based alerts and to metrics-based ones. This has been a slow effort because it first requires
that the metrics exist in order to create the alerts. Up to this point, instrumenting an
application with metrics has been left up to the application teams, and the result has been that
the progress on migrating away from log-based alerts has been slow.
The team doesn't see how it will be possible to meet some of the objectives of the project and
still allow log-based alerts for customer-facing services. While the effort to migrate off of those
types of alerts has been slow, the team agrees that they will need to find a way to entice or force
the application teams to make the needed changes. Limiting the scope of this change should
help get the support needed for the effort from senior management, but the work will still have
to go into an application team's backlog and be prioritized with other work. They decide to
present a plan to senior leadership, calling for the completion of this work by customer-facing
applications only within a year.

Let's look at how fraud detection and response could be enhanced with AIOps. Through this

The use case: As a fraud specialist, I want automated alerting, incident response, and ticket
augmentation for potential fraud activity.

Notifying the account owner and asking them to call in

There are a few other requirements here that may not be as immediately obvious. Most

monetary investment to make into security. That model sets the threshold for optimal
maximum investment at 37% of the expected loss from a breach (https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Gordon%E2%80%93Loeb_model).

For this use case, the AIOps system will have an immediate and measurable impact on the end

critical to get this right, and use a crawl, walk, run approach.
The first step is working with all dependent teams to get the data needed by the fraud
department with the correct enrichment. This isn't an easy or overnight process. So, it may not

processes of the company to ensure proper prioritization of the work. Demonstrating potential

While that data enrichment doesn't exist, it's possible to start satisfying the definition of done

accessible to the AI agent. If access is via an API call, then the agent will need to be given an

server, our first one.
Where the automation isn't doing a great job today is in augmenting the incident ticket with
all the relevant data. Financial systems data is highly regulated, so correlating it could be
challenging. However, if we consider a data model for event metrics, it's likely that there is a
one-way hash for correlating the idx_dab8451e metric to the account. Therefore, the AI agent can find
relevant metrics and logs, keying off that hash, and identify other potentially useful data
points to key off of, such as the typical time of day for user activity. It can combine raw data
with an analysis of that data and write it to the ticketing system.
